# Blog

The home page lists thirteen published CMS essays with linked titles, excerpts, enriched author names, dates and tags. It also provides CMS search and pagination beneath a shared site header.

The posts form an alternating Jenny-and-Jonny sequence about living slowly with fast technology. The latest early-autumn group covers an old wireless radio, repairing a garden gate with online instructions, and a shared digital calendar remembering an obsolete reminder.

All posts use `country-life`, `technology` and `attention`; matching taxonomy records exist for all three tags.

**Build mechanics:** CMS Search plus a CMS Collection bound to `cms/posts`; collection copy is driven by item frontmatter and Markdown bodies rather than static page nodes. Author and tag data are enriched from sibling CMS folders. The page requires PHP.

# CMS Content Model

Posts use frontmatter tag arrays whose lowercase slugs match sibling records under `cms/tags`. Those records enrich each slug into runtime objects exposing fields including `title` and `url`. Authors are similarly enriched from `cms/authors`.

The current taxonomy contains ten records: `personal`, `technology`, `country-life`, `attention`, `home`, `nature`, `communication`, `memory`, `habit`, and `repair`. Every tag assigned to a post has a corresponding taxonomy record.

Runtime CMS values are rendered with Twig. Inside custom components, Twig must be enclosed by Elements Language `@raw()` / `@endraw` so it survives build-time processing.

# Slow Life, Fast Technology

The blog’s central editorial thread: Jenny and Jonny examine how technology changes attention, relationships, work and the texture of an ordinary day in the English countryside.

Stories begin with a concrete moment—often in the cottage, garden or village—and widen into a question. The position is curious and balanced rather than anti-technology. Recurring anchors include the kitchen window’s unreliable signal, tea, breakfast, birds, weather, local journeys and modest experiments with digital habits.

## Opening sequence

1. **The Signal at the Kitchen Window** — Jenny introduces the cottage, its unreliable connection and the question of attention.
2. **The Quiet Hour** — Jonny tries beginning the day without a screen.
3. **Rain in the Forecast** — Jenny compares weather apps with looking directly at the sky.
4. **The Road the Map Forgot** — Jonny follows a sat-nav route to a locked farm gate.
5. **News from the Village Chat** — Jenny considers online availability and neighbourliness.
6. **A Sensor in the Shed** — Jonny over-engineers a simple light switch.
7. **The Photo and the Moment** — Jenny asks when recording an experience begins to interrupt it.
8. **The Update That Could Have Waited** — Jonny loses an evening to a supposedly quick software update.
9. **Voices Across the Distance** — Jenny explores technology as a genuine bridge to distant family.
10. **When the Lights Went Out** — Jonny brings the first sequence together during a village power cut.
11. **Voices from the Wireless** — Jenny finds companionship and useful unpredictability in an old radio.
12. **How to Mend a Gate** — Jonny combines online advice with practical judgement to repair the garden gate.
13. **The Calendar Remembers** — Jenny considers how digital calendars preserve intentions after life has changed around them.
14. **The App That Knew the Way** — Jonny lets a cycling app divide a familiar country lane into measured intervals.
15. **The Long Email** — Jenny rediscovers the generosity and attention contained in unhurried correspondence.
16. **The Thing in the Freezer** — Jonny tests whether an inventory app can solve a problem better handled with masking tape.

The authors alternate throughout. Later posts recall earlier details—the kitchen window, quiet hour, weather, village chat, smart shed and power cut—without requiring readers to follow the sequence strictly.

Tagging now uses varied, topic-specific combinations drawn from ten valid taxonomy records rather than assigning the same broad trio to nearly every essay. The focused taxonomy covers technology, attention, country life, home, nature, communication, memory, habit, repair and personal writing.

title: Project Knowledge
summary: Index of all project knowledge pages
---

This is the AI-maintained knowledge base for this project, following the Karpathy compiled-knowledge pattern. The LLM reads live pages once and compiles them into an interlinked graph of notes. Subsequent sessions read the notes, not the live pages — answers compound rather than being re-derived each time.

## Note graph

The knowledge graph lives in four folders. Use `[[folder/note]]` wikilinks for cross-references between notes.

- **pages/** — one note per live RapidWeaver page; keyed on `pageId`; records purpose, sections, components, and summary in the user's voice
- **concepts/** — themes and patterns spanning multiple pages (e.g. "testimonials pattern", "pricing section")
- **entities/** — people, clients, tools, custom components, publishing destinations
- **analyses/** — durable answers to synthesis questions; filed when a query answer is worth preserving

### When to create a concept or entity note

Create a note proactively — do not wait to be asked:

- **entities/**: any named person appearing in a role (officer, winner, organiser, contact); any named event, race, trophy, award, or external tool/service.
- **concepts/**: any structural or content pattern that appears across 3 or more pages (e.g. same image+link layout, recurring winner table structure, recurring membership pricing model).

Use a lowercase hyphenated slug (e.g. `entities/ian-wright.md`, `concepts/photo-album-pattern.md`). Add a `## See also` section with `[[folder/note]]` wikilinks back to every page note that references it, and add the reciprocal link in each of those page notes.

### Page note format

```yaml
---
title: Page Title
type: page          # page | concept | entity | analysis
pageId: <uuid>      # for type:page — the Elements page UUID (stable across sessions)
path: /slug         # site path
lastIngested: YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MMZ
sources: []         # [[links]] to notes this draws from
tags: []
concerns:           # known problems, tech debt, or gotchas for this page/concept
  - "Brief description of the issue (severity: low|medium|high)"
---

# Page Title

Summary in the user's voice. Sections, components used, index/sitemap flags.

**Build mechanics** (required — record HOW things are built, not just WHAT they render): list the element types used, any custom components and how many instances, whether data is hardcoded or driven by CMS/properties, and whether styling uses design-system tokens or bypasses them (e.g. "12 per-year hand-edited HTML custom components; data hardcoded in template; colours bypass Tailwind tokens").

## See also
- [[concepts/related-concept]]
- [[entities/entity-name]]
```

- **[style-visual.md](style-visual.md)** — layout and visual conventions; read via `getDesignSystem` before building pages

## Project admin

- **[overview.md](overview.md)** — site purpose, target audience, and high-level structure
- **[journal.md](journal.md)** — append-only session log (newest entries at top)
- **[concerns.md](concerns.md)** — known problems, tech debt, gotchas, and fragile areas (derived from per-note `concerns:` frontmatter + `lintKnowledge`; regenerated on close)
- **[backlog.md](backlog.md)** — outstanding work and speculative ideas with priority and status
- **[services.md](services.md)** — external services, APIs, and integrations
- **[field-reports/](field-reports/)** — structured AI session blocker reports; summaries linked from concerns.md

## Operations

Three recurring workflows — all orchestrated by the LLM using the storage primitives above.

**Ingest** (triggered by drift or new page): `getPageMarkdown(pageId)` → `editKnowledge` writePage `pages/<slug>.md` with `pageId` + `lastIngested` → touch/create linked `concepts/` and `entities/` notes → add `[[folder/note]]` wikilinks both directions and `## See also` → refresh `index.md`. If the page reveals a new voice or visual convention, call `updateDesignSystem` to reconcile the design guides.

**Query**: read `index.md` → relevant notes (re-ingest only if `stale: true`) → synthesise with `[[folder/note]]` wikilinks as citations → optionally file durable answer as `analyses/<slug>.md`. **Exception — architecture/improvement requests**: for any "how do I improve", "review", or "what's wrong with" question, always inspect the live document first (`listCustomComponents` + a sample `getCustomComponent` + `getPageContent` on representative pages) before answering, regardless of note freshness. Rank findings by altitude: maintainability/structure → design-system → content. Record findings into per-note `concerns:` and regenerate `concerns.md`.

**Lint**: call `lintKnowledge` → act on orphans, broken links, stale notes, dangling page notes, index drift → fix and log.

## Purpose

A shared personal blog by Jenny and Jonny, a couple living in the English countryside and trying to make sense of the modern world and technology. Posts use ordinary domestic and rural moments to explore attention, convenience, connection and the choices hidden inside everyday tools.

## Target Audience

Readers who enjoy reflective personal essays, countryside observations and thoughtful but non-technical writing about digital life. The blog welcomes people who use and value technology while questioning how it shapes their days.

## Editorial Structure

Jenny and Jonny alternate or respond to one another. Each post stands alone but shares recurring places, objects and questions, creating an ongoing conversation around [[concepts/slow-life-fast-technology]].

The opening pair is “The Signal at the Kitchen Window” by [[entities/jenny]] and “The Quiet Hour” by [[entities/jonny]].

## Site Structure

The Blog page lists CMS posts. Post displays individual essays. Tags and Authors provide taxonomy routes, Archive provides a chronological index, About introduces the publication, and Admin hosts the CMS editor.

title: Writing Style
summary: Voice and tone guide — read before authoring any copy
---

## Voice & Tone

Warm, observant and lightly wry. The blog is written by Jenny and Jonny, a couple living in the English countryside and trying to make sense of everyday life, attention and technology. It should feel thoughtful rather than preachy, curious rather than certain, and grounded in lived moments rather than abstract advice.

## Sentence Rhythm

Mix clear medium-length reflections with occasional short paragraphs for emphasis. Open with a concrete domestic or rural detail, move towards a wider question, and finish on a modest image or thought rather than a grand conclusion.

## Vocabulary

Use natural British English: “countryside”, “kettle”, “post”, “weather”, “garden”, “train”. Favour sensory specifics, gentle understatement and affectionate humour. Technology language should remain accessible and tied to ordinary use.

Avoid productivity jargon, sweeping claims, generic tutorials, anti-technology moralising, and presenting either author as an expert with all the answers.

## Person & POV

First person singular for an authored post, with natural references to the other partner and occasional “we” for their shared life. Jenny’s voice is perceptive, reflective and attentive to place. Jonny’s is practical, dryly humorous and inclined to test small ideas. They may refer back to one another’s posts so the blog reads as an ongoing conversation.

## Common Thread

The central editorial thread is **living slowly with fast technology**: how devices, software and the internet alter attention, relationships, work and the texture of an ordinary day in the English countryside. Recurring anchors include the cottage kitchen, the unreliable signal, tea and breakfast, birds, weather, local travel and small household experiments.

Posts should connect loosely through repeated places, objects or questions. Each piece needs to stand alone while advancing the shared inquiry. Neither author rejects technology; both look for a more deliberate relationship with it.

## Heading Style

Sentence-style literary titles, usually concrete and understated: “The Signal at the Kitchen Window”, “The Quiet Hour”. Avoid listicle and search-optimised constructions unless deliberately subverted.

## Caption & Label Style

Brief, descriptive and understated. Use sentence case. Keep labels functional and captions observational rather than promotional.

## See also
- [[style-visual]]
- [[concepts/slow-life-fast-technology]]
- [[entities/jenny]]
- [[entities/jonny]]

title: The Signal at the Kitchen Window
date: 2025-08-06
author: Jenny
tags:
  - home
  - technology
  - attention
excerpt: A first note from our cottage, where the internet works best beside the kitchen window and the slower pace is beginning to change how we see technology.
---

There is one particular spot beside our kitchen window where the internet works properly. If I balance the laptop between the bread bin and a pot of rosemary, messages arrive, pages load and the wider world comes rushing back in.

Two steps towards the kettle and it all becomes uncertain again.

Jonny and I moved to this corner of the English countryside expecting mud, quiet and a slightly unreasonable number of spiders. We did not expect the patchy signal to become such a useful measure of our attention.

In the city, being connected felt like the natural state of things. Here, it is an event. A delivery van appears at the gate. The church clock marks the hour. A phone finds one bar and immediately begins reporting everything we have missed.

At first, I treated these interruptions as problems to solve. I moved the router, tested cables and stood in several undignified positions with my phone held above my head. But lately I have begun to wonder whether the inconvenience is trying to tell us something.

Technology promises to remove friction, yet a little friction can make a choice visible. Do I really need to check this now? Am I looking something up, or simply looking away? Would the thought survive until after breakfast?

This blog is our place to work through those questions. Not as experts, and certainly not as people who have escaped modern life. We like useful gadgets, good software and knowing when the train is delayed. We are simply curious about how all this technology changes the shape of an ordinary day.

Outside the window, a wren is dismantling the moss around the drainpipe. Inside, the laptop has lost the signal again.

For the moment, I think I will let it.

title: The Quiet Hour
date: 2025-08-08
author: Jonny
tags:
  - habit
  - country-life
  - attention
excerpt: After Jenny’s kitchen-window revelation, Jonny tries beginning the day without a screen and discovers that a quiet hour is not quite the same as an empty one.
---

Two mornings after Jenny wrote about the signal by the kitchen window, I found her note open on the laptop beside the bread bin.

My first instinct was to check whether anyone had read it.

That seemed to prove her point rather neatly, so I closed the lid and made tea instead.

We have started calling the time before breakfast “the quiet hour”. The name makes it sound more disciplined than it is. There are no rules pinned to the fridge and no matching linen outfits. We simply try not to look at a screen until we have opened the curtains, fed the birds and decided what sort of weather the sky is attempting.

This morning it could not make up its mind. Mist sat low over the field, the hedge dripped steadily, and somewhere beyond the garden a tractor started with the weary determination of an old desktop computer.

Without the phone, I noticed how many small urges arrive dressed as necessities. Check the forecast. Read the news. See whether that parcel has moved. Look up the name of the bird on the fence. Each thought feels urgent for roughly twelve seconds, then wanders off if it is not fed.

The bird, incidentally, was probably a dunnock. I looked it up later.

I do not think the answer is to reject technology. Our work depends on it, our family lives far away, and yesterday an app stopped us driving twenty miles towards a closed road. But convenience has a way of becoming the background against which everything else must compete.

The quiet hour is a small experiment in changing that background. The internet will still be there after toast. The messages will keep. The world can begin without our immediate supervision.

By half past eight, Jenny was at the kitchen window with the laptop and I was checking the rain radar. We had not transformed ourselves. We had only made a little room at the start of the day.

For now, that feels like enough.

title: Rain in the Forecast
date: 2025-08-11
author: Jenny
status: published
tags:
  - country-life
  - technology
  - nature
excerpt: Three weather apps disagree about the afternoon, while the swallows over the field offer a forecast of their own.
---

At seven this morning, the three weather apps on my phone offered three different versions of the afternoon.

One promised sunshine. One showed rain beginning at two. The third had placed a small grey cloud over the village and seemed unwilling to commit itself further.

Outside, the swallows were flying low over the field.

My grandmother would have considered that sufficient information. Jonny, who had washing on the line and therefore more at stake, refreshed the radar.

Since beginning our quiet hour, I have become more aware of the way information enters a day. A forecast ought to help us prepare, but the more often I checked it, the less prepared I felt. Each update produced a new future to consider: walk now, wait until later, bring in the washing, leave it another ten minutes.

The sky, meanwhile, continued being the sky.

Living here has not made me wise about weather. I still leave windows open at the wrong moment and own a raincoat that is usually hanging wherever I am not. But I am learning that uncertainty feels different when you look at it directly.

The clouds above the beech trees were dark at their edges. The air had that close, metallic stillness that makes the leaves appear to be listening. None of this told me whether rain would begin at two fourteen, but it told me enough to take a coat.

There is a kind of confidence in precise data. A little blue line moves across a map and gives the impression that the afternoon has already happened somewhere else. Often it is wonderfully useful. Last winter, a flood alert gave our neighbour time to move his car. Today, though, the hourly percentages became another thing to tend.

At half past one, Jonny brought in the washing. At twenty to two, the sun came out. He gave me a look that suggested the swallows had let us both down.

Then, just after three, rain arrived in a sudden silver sheet. It struck the kitchen window, flattened the rosemary and briefly silenced the internet.

We made tea and stood in the doorway watching it bounce off the path.

The apps had not been wrong, exactly. Nor had the birds. The trouble was my hope that one of them might remove the need to notice what was happening.

Tomorrow’s forecast says clear skies.

I will still look out of the window.

title: The Road the Map Forgot
date: 2025-08-14
author: Jonny
status: published
tags:
  - nature
  - country-life
  - technology
excerpt: A sat-nav shortcut ends at a locked farm gate and raises the awkward question of when directions become decisions.
---

The sat-nav announced that we had arrived while we were facing a locked farm gate.

Beyond it stood three cows, a stack of wrapped hay bales and no obvious sign of the garden centre Jenny had been promised.

“Perhaps it’s a very exclusive garden centre,” I said.

Jenny looked at the map. The blue route continued confidently through the gate, across the field and, as far as we could tell, into a pond.

We had set out for a bag of compost and a replacement handle for the kitchen window. The journey should have taken twenty minutes. Forty-five minutes later, we were reversing down a lane barely wider than the car while an elderly spaniel watched from a gateway.

Digital maps are among the bits of technology I would defend without much hesitation. They have rescued us from ring roads, found petrol stations at inconvenient hours and revealed that the nearest post office is not, in fact, the one in the nearest village.

But they also speak with a certainty the countryside does not always recognise.

A line on a screen may be a road, a track, a private drive or a place where a road was discussed in 1987 and never built. The map knows distance. It does not know that the ford rises after rain, that the lane past the old mill is scraped by hawthorn, or that Mr Turner opens his gate only on market days.

After the farm-gate incident, Jenny found a paper road atlas in the pocket behind my seat. It was six years old and smelled faintly of damp. The garden centre was marked with a pencil circle by whoever owned it before us.

We followed the larger roads and arrived twelve minutes before closing.

On the way home, I thought about the difference between directions and decisions. The sat-nav gives excellent directions, right up until the moment the world disagrees. Then someone must look through the windscreen and decide what sort of road this actually is.

That sounds obvious. Yet I have caught myself obeying the blue line long after the evidence outside has become unpromising. Perhaps certainty is persuasive even when it is sitting in a dashboard and pronouncing local place names incorrectly.

The new window handle cost four pounds. The compost split in the boot.

Later, I reported the missing gate on the map. A small message thanked me for helping improve the route.

I like that. The system did not need abandoning. It needed someone to notice the cows.

title: News from the Village Chat
date: 2025-08-17
author: Jenny
status: published
tags:
  - communication
  - technology
  - attention
excerpt: The village message group delivers a lost hen, a suspicious van and seventeen opinions about the church clock before breakfast.
---

By eight o’clock this morning, the village message group had found a lost hen, identified a suspicious van and produced seventeen opinions about the church clock.

The hen belonged to Paula near the green. The van was delivering a freezer. The clock was four minutes slow, although two people insisted it had always been that way.

When we first moved here, I imagined village news arriving over hedges or beside the shelves in the little shop. Some of it still does. Mrs Evans can communicate an entire planning dispute while choosing tomatoes. But much of the village now lives inside a message thread that never quite sleeps.

It is useful in ways that are difficult to dismiss. We heard about last winter’s fallen tree before setting out. Someone found Jonny’s glove on the footpath and left it in the bus shelter. When an elderly neighbour’s heating stopped, a plumber was at her door within an hour.

It is also capable of turning a blurry photograph of tyre tracks into a public inquiry.

The group has its own weather system. A simple question may pass through helpfulness, speculation, irritation and reconciliation before lunch. People who nod pleasantly at the post box become unexpectedly firm about recycling bins.

I had muted the notifications after the fifth message concerning the church clock, then worried that doing so was unfriendly. This is one of technology’s quieter tricks: it can make availability feel like kindness. If a message has reached us, perhaps we ought to respond. If we do not respond, perhaps we have failed some small test of neighbourliness.

But a village is not the same thing as its chat.

This afternoon I walked to the green and found Paula scattering corn beside a hedge. Her hen, Mabel, had returned on her own and was behaving as though the morning’s concern had been excessive.

We talked for ten minutes. She told me which blackberries were ready along the lane and warned me that the mobile library had changed its day. Neither fact had appeared in the group.

On the way home, my phone buzzed. Someone wanted to know whether the freezer van was still suspicious.

I typed a reply, deleted it and put the phone back in my pocket.

At the cottage, Jonny was adjusting the kitchen clock. It was four minutes slow.

“Apparently it has always been like that,” I told him.

He left it alone.

title: A Sensor in the Shed
date: 2025-08-20
author: Jonny
status: published
tags:
  - technology
  - home
  - habit
excerpt: Jonny automates the shed light, then spends an evening trying to persuade it that he exists.
---

On Tuesday, I installed a motion sensor in the shed.

The shed did not ask for one.

Its existing lighting system consisted of a switch beside the door. You entered, pressed the switch and the light came on. It was reliable, easily understood and had survived at least three previous owners.

Still, the sensor was on offer and promised “effortless illumination”. This seemed attractive. I pictured myself entering with an armful of logs while the shed recognised my presence and welcomed me like a small, timber-built hotel.

Installation took twenty minutes. Configuration took the rest of the evening.

At first the light came on whenever the pear tree moved. Then it refused to come on for me. I adjusted the sensitivity until it could detect a moth at fifteen paces but remained uncertain about a fully grown man standing beneath it and waving a rake.

Jenny watched from the kitchen window.

“Is this saving time?” she called.

“It will,” I said, which is the traditional reply of someone who has already lost an hour.

I like automating things. There is satisfaction in removing a repeated task, however small. A timer switches on the lamp when dusk falls. The heating knows when we are away. Our grocery list appears on both phones, which has reduced the number of times we buy three jars of mustard and no milk.

But automation changes the nature of a failure. When a simple switch fails, you inspect the bulb, the fuse and the switch. When a smart device fails, the problem may be the wireless signal, the settings, an update, an account, a server in another country or the fact that you accidentally created a schedule for Tuesdays in another time zone.

The shed sensor had an app. The app wanted an account. The account wanted a password with a symbol. By the time the light finally responded, darkness had properly fallen and I had forgotten why I went to the shed.

The next morning, I carried out an armful of empty plant pots. The door opened. The light came on. For one perfect moment, the future worked exactly as advertised.

Then a robin flew inside and kept it on for forty minutes.

I have left the sensor in place. This is partly because it now works and partly because removing it would feel like admitting something.

The old switch remains beside the door.

I find that reassuring.

title: The Photo and the Moment
date: 2025-08-23
author: Jenny
status: published
tags:
  - attention
  - memory
  - nature
excerpt: A field full of evening light leaves Jenny wondering when keeping a memory begins to interrupt making one.
---

The field behind the cottage turned gold just before sunset.

Not metaphorically gold, but the brief, unreasonable colour that arrives when low light catches dry grass after rain. Every seed head seemed lit from within. Even the old water trough looked important.

I reached for my phone.

By the time I had opened the camera, dismissed a notification and wiped a fingerprint from the lens, the light had shifted. I took twelve photographs anyway.

None of them looked like the field.

This is not the phone’s fault. The pictures were sharp, correctly exposed and eager to improve themselves. The sky became bluer. The grass gained contrast. A shadow beneath the hedge disappeared. The result was prettier than the scene and less like being there.

I stood by the gate scrolling through the images while the actual evening continued behind the screen.

We photograph so much now because it costs almost nothing. A loaf before it is cut. A dog asleep beneath a table. The first rose. The same rose the following morning with rain on it. Each picture says: keep this.

I understand the impulse. Memory is unreliable and ordinary days vanish quickly. When my mother sends an old photograph, I search its corners for things no one meant to preserve: the wallpaper, a biscuit tin, the shape of a lamp. Often the accidental details matter most.

But collecting a moment can become a way of stepping outside it. I begin arranging the cup rather than drinking the tea. I move until the view is clear of the wheelie bin. I see the evening as a possible image before I feel the cool air on my arms.

Jonny joined me at the gate and asked what I was doing.

“Failing to photograph this,” I said.

He looked at the field. The gold had softened to brown, and a bat was making quick turns above the hedge.

We stayed until the first kitchen lights appeared across the valley.

Later, I kept one photograph. It is slightly blurred and the corner contains Jonny’s sleeve. The field looks flatter than I remember. The sky is the wrong colour.

Yet when I look at it, I can hear the swallows and feel the damp gate beneath my hand.

Perhaps a photograph does not need to contain the moment.

Perhaps it only needs to leave the gate open.

title: The Update That Could Have Waited
date: 2025-08-26
author: Jonny
status: published
tags:
  - technology
  - attention
  - habit
excerpt: A late-night software update, one blinking router and a great deal of misplaced optimism disturb the cottage after dark.
---

At ten forty-seven on Monday night, I pressed a button labelled “Update now”.

This was a mistake.

The laptop had been asking all day. I had declined politely at breakfast, postponed it at lunch and ignored a small red badge through dinner. By bedtime, the message had changed tone. The update was important. It included improvements. Restarting would take only a few minutes.

I believed it.

Jenny went upstairs with a book. I remained at the kitchen table beneath the hard white light of the screen, watching a progress bar reach seventy-three per cent and reconsider its position.

Updates are strange acts of trust. We allow a machine to replace part of itself because someone, somewhere, has decided the new arrangement will be better. Usually it is. Security improves. Faults disappear. A button moves to a place no one expected.

At eleven fifteen, the laptop restarted and lost the internet.

I restarted the router. The router began blinking orange. The kitchen, which had been quiet a moment earlier, filled with the atmosphere of a minor control room.

There is a particular kind of late-night problem-solving that feels heroic while achieving very little. I checked cables. I read support pages on my phone. I discovered several people online who had experienced something similar in 2019.

From upstairs, Jenny called, “Have you tried leaving it until morning?”

This was technically an option, but not one I was ready to consider.

The need to finish was not really about the laptop. It was about restoring the world to the state it had been in before I touched it. Until then, the unresolved problem seemed to occupy the whole cottage.

Just after midnight, the connection returned without explanation. The router turned green. The laptop announced that the update had completed successfully.

Nothing looked different.

The next morning, during the quiet hour, I found a new setting that allows updates to install automatically at a sensible time. I switched it on, then wondered whether this was wisdom or simply another sensor in the shed.

Jenny asked what the update had improved.

I told her the laptop now displayed battery percentage in a slightly different way.

Outside, rainwater dripped from the gutter into a bucket with perfect reliability.

Some systems do not require our supervision.

title: Voices Across the Distance
date: 2025-08-29
author: Jenny
status: published
tags:
  - technology
  - communication
  - personal
excerpt: A video call with family freezes, falters and still manages to make a distant kitchen feel briefly close.
---

My sister’s face froze halfway through a laugh.

For several seconds she remained on the screen with one eyebrow raised and her mouth open, transformed by the internet into an unflattering family portrait.

Then the sound caught up.

We were speaking from two kitchens nearly three hundred miles apart. In hers, my niece was making toast. In ours, Jonny was trying to remain out of view while opening a particularly loud packet of biscuits.

The connection dropped twice. We repeated several sentences. At one point, everyone smiled and nodded without being entirely certain who had spoken.

It was still lovely.

Much of what we write here is about technology asking for too much attention. The notifications, the checking, the sense that every quiet moment ought to be filled. But sometimes a screen does not pull us away from the world. Sometimes it makes a small doorway through it.

When I was younger, a long-distance call was planned. You watched the time and kept an eye on the cost. Photographs arrived after holidays had ended. Ordinary life remained mostly invisible between visits.

Now I can see the new yellow paint in my sister’s kitchen while it is still drying. My niece can carry the phone into the garden to show me a caterpillar. We can be present for things too small to justify a journey and too ordinary to become news.

That ordinariness may be the gift.

A good call is not always a concentrated exchange of important information. It is being left on the counter while someone finds the tea bags. It is hearing a door close in another house. It is Jonny finally appearing with the biscuits and being told they are the wrong kind.

After we said goodbye, the kitchen felt unusually quiet. The screen went dark and reflected our own window, the rosemary pot and a strip of evening sky.

Distance had not disappeared. My sister was still three hundred miles away, and I could not reach across to wipe flour from my niece’s cheek.

But for forty imperfect minutes, our kitchens had shared the same conversation.

The signal at the window held almost all the way through.

title: When the Lights Went Out
date: 2025-09-01
author: Jonny
status: published
tags:
  - country-life
  - home
  - attention
excerpt: A village power cut silences the router, defeats the smart shed and reveals which parts of the evening never needed electricity.
---

The power went out at six seventeen, just as I was putting a tray in the oven.

The oven sighed. The kitchen clock vanished. Somewhere in the shed, the motion sensor surrendered without argument.

For a moment, the cottage became so quiet that we could hear rain ticking against the back door.

I checked the fuse box. Jenny looked out towards the village, where windows were darkening one by one. My phone still had a signal, so I opened the electricity company’s website. It confirmed there was a power cut in our area and estimated restoration by nine.

This was useful information. I checked it again five minutes later in case the nature of electricity had changed.

Without the router, the house felt oddly disconnected from its usual background activity. No radio in the kitchen. No small lights on chargers. No laptop pretending to be asleep. Even the fridge had stopped its occasional muttering.

We found candles in the drawer where batteries, string and things without obvious homes accumulate. Jenny lit two. I attempted to rescue dinner on the camping stove, which turned a planned vegetable bake into a pan of warm, argumentative ingredients.

The village chat became extremely active. People reported streets without power to other people on the same streets. Someone asked whether the church clock had stopped. Paula posted that Mabel the hen was safe, though no one had enquired.

Then my phone battery reached twelve per cent.

I put it face down.

We ate at the kitchen table by candlelight. This sounds romantic. In practice, I dropped a carrot on the floor and Jenny could not tell whether the sauce looked right. Still, the darkness changed the size of the room. The windows became mirrors. The table, the candles and the two of us seemed to be the whole available world.

We talked about the past few weeks: the quiet hour, the wrong road, the field at sunset, the laptop update. None of our experiments had produced a rule worth framing. We still checked the weather too often. The shed remained needlessly intelligent. Jenny had taken six photographs of the candles before dinner.

But we had begun to notice the moments when convenience became compulsion, and the moments when technology genuinely carried us towards someone else.

At eight fifty-three, every light in the cottage returned at once.

The fridge woke. The router blinked. The oven demanded to know the time.

I picked up my phone, then left it on the table for another minute.

Outside, the rain had stopped. Across the field, the village windows came back one by one, each a small square of yellow in the dark.

title: Voices from the Wireless
date: 2025-09-04
author: Jenny
status: published
tags:
  - technology
  - home
  - attention
excerpt: After the power cut, an old kitchen radio reminds Jenny that not every connection needs a screen, an account or her immediate reply.
---

Three days after the power cut, I found an old radio at the back of the pantry.

It was wedged behind a stack of jars and a cake tin containing no cake. The plastic had yellowed slightly, and the aerial extended with the careful reluctance of an elderly umbrella.

Jonny put in two batteries. Nothing happened.

He turned one of the batteries around. The radio crackled into life with a discussion about turnips.

We left it on while making breakfast.

There was something pleasantly undemanding about the voices in the kitchen. They did not arrive with pictures, comments or a row of related stories. No small red number indicated how much listening remained. We could pay attention, drift away, return halfway through a sentence and discover that the turnips had become train delays.

The radio made no effort to know us.

Most of the technology we use now improves itself by learning who we are. It remembers what we watched, where we travelled and which songs we skipped after eleven seconds. This can be wonderfully convenient. It can also make the world feel like a corridor lined with versions of our previous choices.

The old radio offered whatever happened to be on.

At nine, there was local news. A bridge would close for repairs. The village fête had raised more than expected. Someone had seen an unusual bird near the reservoir, though the presenter sounded unconvinced.

None of it had been selected for me, and perhaps that was why I listened.

Later, music filled the kitchen while I peeled apples. I did not know the singer. I could have held up my phone and asked it to identify the song, but the phone was in the other room and my hands were sticky.

So I let the song remain unknown.

This felt surprisingly difficult. Information is usually so close that not knowing can seem like unfinished business. A bird must be named. A tune must be found. A half-remembered actor must be identified before the kettle boils.

The song ended. Another began. The moment closed without being solved.

By lunchtime, the radio had developed a faint hiss. Jonny adjusted the aerial and accidentally found a station broadcasting a gardening phone-in. A caller from Norfolk was worried about her courgettes.

We listened to the answer as though it might matter to us.

Outside, the first leaves were gathering beneath the kitchen window. The radio crackled softly beside the bread bin, asking nothing and keeping us company.

title: How to Mend a Gate
date: 2025-09-07
author: Jonny
status: published
tags:
  - repair
  - country-life
  - technology
excerpt: Jonny takes a phone, three online tutorials and unjustified confidence to a sagging garden gate.
---

The garden gate had been dragging across the path since July.

Each time I opened it, the bottom corner carved a pale curve through the gravel. Each time I closed it, I lifted slightly and promised myself I would fix it at the weekend.

Several weekends passed in this way.

On Sunday, I took my phone, a box of tools and an unjustified sense of confidence into the garden.

A search for “how to fix a sagging wooden gate” produced thousands of results. Some suggested tightening the hinges. Others recommended a diagonal brace, a cable kit or complete replacement. One man repaired a gate larger than our cottage using equipment that appeared to belong on a building site.

I watched three videos and became briefly knowledgeable.

This is one of the internet’s real wonders. Somewhere, someone has encountered almost any practical problem and explained it clearly while wearing work trousers. A leaking tap, a bicycle gear, a mysterious mark on a tomato leaf: the answer is usually waiting, recorded by a patient stranger in a well-lit garage.

The difficulty is knowing which stranger has your gate.

In the first video, the hinges opened in the opposite direction. In the second, the post was concrete. The third began with the words, “This is a very straightforward job,” which I have learnt to treat as a warning.

Jenny brought tea and found me holding a spirit level against a post that was visibly leaning.

“What have you discovered?” she asked.

“That the post is not level.”

“I had noticed it was attached to the gate.”

The useful advice turned out to be the least dramatic: support the gate, loosen the bolts, raise the hinge and tighten everything again. I propped one corner on two old gardening books, selected a spanner and tried not to think about what would happen if the post moved.

It worked.

For nearly ten minutes, the gate swung freely. Then the top hinge made a small metallic sound and the corner dropped back into the gravel.

I returned to the videos.

By late afternoon, I had fitted a larger washer and replaced one tired bolt. The gate opened without scraping. It closed with a firm wooden click that was far more satisfying than the scale of the achievement justified.

The repair came from several places: a video made in Yorkshire, a forum comment from 2016, the contents of our shed and Jenny’s suggestion that I stop adjusting the wrong hinge.

Technology had not done the job for me. It had placed a crowd of distant people beside the gate.

As I packed away the tools, the motion sensor switched on the shed light in broad daylight.

Some projects remain ongoing.

title: The Calendar Remembers
date: 2025-09-10
author: Jenny
status: published
tags:
  - technology
  - memory
  - home
excerpt: An old reminder in the shared calendar reveals how efficiently technology preserves plans—and how little it understands change.
---

On Tuesday morning, our shared calendar reminded us to collect the keys to the cottage.

We had collected them more than a year ago.

The notification appeared at nine, bright and punctual, as though we were still standing outside an estate agent with a cardboard box of mugs in the car. Jonny looked at his phone, then at the kitchen around us.

“We seem to have done it,” he said.

I had forgotten creating the reminder. The calendar had not.

It also remembers dentist appointments, birthdays, the day the bins change after a bank holiday and an optimistic annual instruction to clean the gutters. It carries our future in coloured blocks and sends small warnings as each piece approaches.

Most of the time, this is helpful. Without it, we would miss trains, double-book weekends and remember the boiler service only when the boiler developed a personality.

But the old reminder made me think about the way a calendar preserves intention.

When I entered “Collect cottage keys”, the words contained a whole imagined life. We had not yet learnt where the morning light reached the kitchen, which floorboard creaked outside the bedroom or how often leaves would block the drain. The shed had an ordinary switch. The village chat did not know our names. The kitchen window was simply a window, not the most reliable place to reach the internet.

A calendar records the event but not what happened to it afterwards.

Scrolling back, I found plans we had cancelled because of rain and dinners with people who have since moved away. There were reminders to buy paint for a room we eventually left white. A weekend marked “sort garden” appeared during the month when we mostly watched the garden become wetter.

The entries looked definite, though the life around them had been anything but.

Technology is very good at keeping the promises we make to the future. It cannot tell which ones still matter.

I deleted the reminder about the keys. For a moment, this felt oddly like erasing the day itself. Then I looked at the chipped blue key bowl by the door and remembered that the evidence was everywhere.

The calendar still contains next Saturday’s village apple day, Jonny’s appointment with the dentist and a note to bring the washing in before rain.

That last one is mine.

The forecast says sunshine, but I have learnt not to leave these things entirely to memory—or to the forecast.

title: The App That Knew the Way
date: 2025-09-13
author: Jonny
status: published
tags:
  - country-life
  - technology
  - nature
  - habit
excerpt: A cycling app plots a route through lanes Jonny has known for years, and he follows it anyway.
---

I have cycled the lane past Hartley Farm perhaps forty times.

I know where the surface breaks at the dip after the oak tree. I know that the last quarter-mile rises gradually enough to feel flat until the moment it does not. I know the corner where a collie appears at a gap in the fence and gives a brief opinion of cyclists before losing interest entirely.

On Saturday, I set out with a new cycling app and followed its instructions.

It sent me the same way.

The app had a map, a blue line, a small animated figure that represented me and a series of encouraging messages about my pace. It knew the distance, the elevation, the estimated time and my current heart rate. It did not know about the collie.

I am not sure why I opened the app at all. The route was familiar. I had no particular goal, no distance to measure and no one waiting for the data. Perhaps it was habit. Perhaps the phone felt incomplete in my jersey pocket without something running.

The fields were dry and loud with the end of summer. Tractor ruts had hardened in the gateway mud. The hedgerows were heavy with haws and the beginnings of sloe, the kind of dark purple that always looks implausible. The app announced that I had cycled three kilometres.

Somewhere around the four-kilometre mark, it offered a small vibration and a badge.

I had earned the badge for cycling on a Saturday. This seemed a low bar, but I appreciated the encouragement.

What struck me was not the data itself but the way it divided the ride. Without the app, the lane is a single continuous thing: the farm, the oak, the rise, the return. The app turned it into intervals. Each kilometre arrived as an event. My attention moved between the hedgerow and the screen on my wrist.

This is not a complaint. The data was accurate. The badge was unambiguous. And when I reached the top of the hill and found the view west across the valley — the light-bleached stubble fields, the village below, a kite circling without apparent effort — I put my wrist down and simply looked.

The app ticked quietly.

At the gate I usually lean against to drink water, I stopped and tried to remember whether I had noticed the haws before the first kilometre announcement or after it. I could not quite place it.

Jenny suggests that I am inclined to complicate straightforward pleasures. This may be true. But I think the complication was already there in the pocket. The question is only whether to open the app or leave it closed.

On the way home, I turned the screen off.

The lane was exactly as long as it had always been. The collie was at its fence. I stood on the pedals for the final corner, which has no data attached to it at all.

The badge remains. I cycled on a Saturday and a machine noted the fact.

I find I am glad the kite was not in the app.

excerpt: A friend sends a proper letter in the form of an email, and Jenny realises how long she has been replying in a different language.
---

My friend Sarah sent me an email last Tuesday that took me twelve minutes to read.

Not because it was difficult. Because there was a great deal in it.

She wrote about her allotment, a television programme she had started and abandoned, a book she had finished and pressed on her mother, a visit to a cathedral that had moved her unexpectedly, and a thought she had been carrying since we last met in April and had not known how to raise until now. She had composed it, apparently, across three evenings.

I sat at the kitchen table and read it twice.

The second reading was slower. I kept stopping at sentences — not because they were complex, but because they were generous. She had trusted me with the unhurried version of her life. No emoji, no brevity, no message thread where words dissolve under the next reply. Just twelve minutes of Sarah, thinking carefully.

I realised, somewhere in the second paragraph about the allotment, that I had not written anything like it in months.

The messages I send have grown shorter without my noticing. A response becomes a reaction. A question becomes a tick. I have begun to feel that the medium prefers speed, and I have adjusted myself accordingly. When a reply takes thought, I leave it to draft and return to it later, which often means the later becomes never.

Sarah's email had done the thing a long letter does: it made me aware of how much usually goes unsaid.

Jonny asked what I was reading. I described it poorly — “a long email from Sarah” — as though length were the point. The real thing I was struggling to describe was that it felt like a visit.

I went upstairs to the desk and wrote back.

I had not sat at the desk for correspondence since we moved. It is normally occupied by seed catalogues, a box of batteries with unclear remaining charge and the manual for the shed sensor, which Jonny consults periodically without apparent benefit. But the desk has a window looking over the apple tree, and that afternoon the light was soft and the apples were beginning to blush at their shoulders, and it seemed the right place.

I wrote for about an hour. I told her about the cottage, the quiet hour, the radio we found after the power cut. I described the field at sunset that I had failed to photograph. I mentioned the calendar reminder that appeared for a day that had already happened. I said things I had been carrying since April without knowing it.

When I finished, the light had shifted and there was a smell of rain on the way.

I pressed send and sat for a moment. The machine was instant, as always. Sarah's allotment was three hundred miles from my apple tree, but the email would arrive before the rain.

Technology had not slowed any of this down. I had.

Perhaps there is a kind of attention that the medium cannot give you, only reflect back. The long email was possible because Sarah chose to take the time. The reply was possible because I sat down and began.

Jonny found me at the desk and offered tea. He looked at the screen.

“Did you write all that?”

“Sarah wrote first,” I said.

He nodded as though this explained something.

The rain arrived twenty minutes later. The apple tree shook once and was still.

title: The Thing in the Freezer
date: 2025-09-19
author: Jonny
status: published
tags:
  - habit
  - technology
  - home
  - attention
excerpt: A freezer inventory app promises to end mystery meals, and Jonny spends a weekend testing whether the problem needed solving.
---

At the back of our freezer, behind a bag of broad beans and something in foil that may have been soup, I found a container labelled “Aug?” in Jenny's handwriting.

It was, in the end, a very good ratatouille.

But the question mark had bothered me for a week, so I did what I usually do when a small problem catches my attention: I downloaded an app.

The freezer inventory app was straightforward in principle. You enter each item when it goes in, with a quantity, a date and a category. The app tells you what you have, reminds you when things are approaching the end of their useful life and prevents the slow accumulation of mystery containers at the back.

I spent Saturday morning entering the current contents.

This required defrosting one corner, which required moving things onto the kitchen table, which revealed that we owned four bags of frozen peas at various stages of completeness, two unlabelled blocks that turned out to be stock, a bag of frozen cranberries from Christmas and a container of leftover curry that was already in the app on my phone before I remembered I had started this before.

Jenny watched from the doorway with a cup of tea.

“You're solving the label problem by not labelling things,” she observed.

This was technically accurate. I was photographing containers and typing descriptions rather than writing on them. The result was the same information in a less accessible format.

The app worked as described. It remembered everything, sorted by category and sent a notification about the broad beans, which I acknowledged and then ignored. Within a few days I had forgotten to update it when we used the stock, so the app believed we had more than we did. I corrected this. Then forgot again.

By the end of the second week, the app contained a confident and partly fictional account of our freezer.

The original problem — the question mark, the occasional uncertainty about the broad beans — had not been a failure of information management. It had been a failure of labelling, which requires only a pen, a piece of masking tape and the thirty seconds I usually spend pressing the container into available space and hoping for the best.

Jenny suggested masking tape. I pointed out that she had also written “Aug?”.

We agreed that this was a shared habit rather than a technical challenge.

The app is still on my phone. I have updated it once since writing this, which is probably enough. It is good software. It is organised, clear and free. The broad beans remain.

What it could not do was make labelling feel worth doing in the moment. That is not the app's fault. The moment always passes quickly, the freezer is cold and the ratatouille is still hot and the pen is in a drawer.

I have put a pen on top of the freezer.

Jenny has already borrowed it.

The next container to go in will say “Sept” without a question mark. This is, I think, the level of record-keeping our freezer actually requires. No reminder. No category. No photograph.

Just the month and a reasonable confidence in the cook.
